I" InEiir EUl HALL FIRE 


“Lisa and Bruce! The Dining Hall is 
burning! I’m not kidding!” Slam went the 
door. 

That was our wake up call three 
mornings before our campers arrived. We 
ran out the door, looked up, and saw the 
most enormous roaring, ball of fire 
imaginable. Obviously the fire was out of 
control and far too hot to approach. All 
we could do was try to contain it. It was 
about 5:45 a.m. perfectly still, and 
drizzling rain — the weather was on our 
side! Thankfully, the building had fields 
on two sides, the third had a road behind 
it and then a utility building (it didn’t 
burn), the fourth side had a small bush — 
therefore our main worry. Our staff, at 
camp for Pre-Camp training, were 
fantastic despite a flu bug that was 
making its rounds. All fire fighting 
equipment in camp was gathered and 
organized in a couple of minutes. An 
assembly line for water buckets from the 
lake up a long hill to the Dining Hall was 
formed — about 200 yards long. 
Buildings close by were sprayed from 
hand pumps, and the bush area was 
similarly covered. The volunteer fire 
department of both Oso and 
Hichinbrooke Townships were at camp 
within a short 12 minutes. Their efforts 
and concern were tremendous. However, 
the Dining Hall was completely destroyed. 
No other buildings, or activity sites were 
lost. The Hall prepared and fed meals for 
over 300. It was beautiful, the nicest 
building in camp, 20 years old. Gone. 
Absolutely nothing left but three stone 
fireplaces. 

Once the fire was under control the 
enormity started to hit!: 

— three hundred bodies to feed in 3 
days; no food and no place to feed 
them 

— a lot of camp memorabilia — gone 

— all equipment and food gone 

I can remember saying to myself several 
times — you’re lucky no one was hurt! 
So, what do we do now? 

First, we needed breakfast for eighty, 
chilly and challenged staff. We tele¬ 
phoned the local grocery store and told 
them our plight. They were very helpful 
even at 7:00 a.m. We sent up our truck 
with two people and loaded it up with 
bread, P.B. and J., fresh oranges, coffee 
and hot chocolate. We didn’t have a 
toaster, but fortunately some of our staff 
had electric kettles. Our dishes, of course, 
were gone, but enough were scrounged up 
in the Trip Room and from personal staff 
dishes intended for picnics and canoe 
trips. 

We telephoned people that we knew 
that might have been able to help. We 
certainly used many of our connections! 


At a time like this you need all the help 
you can get, friends stand up with flags 
willing to do anything possible. We 
needed to feed 300 people in three days, 
we needed some special resources. 

The Army was a big help to us, they 
were able to supply stoves, tables and 
chairs for three hundred. They did what¬ 
ever they could after they were sure that 
all civilian resources were tapped. We 
therefore had to pay a nominal fee. 

We also telephoned A.T.C.O. which is 
a company that supplies portable kitchen 
and dining facilities for various groups 
such as lumber and mining camps. We 
were able to get a six tractor trailer unit, 
three for kitchen and three for dining. 
These were put up side by side and the 
walls were removed in-between, it then 
looked like one large room. There were 
certainly problems getting the units down 
and set up — most problems being trans¬ 
portation due to the long weekend and 
unionized days of travel. The re-hook- 
up at our end was a wee nightmare but it 
all worked out in the end. We also used 
one of our smaller lodges, nearby, to 
alleviate some of the crowding. Before the 
hook up was complete (for two weeks) we 
ate in two shifts per meal, the cooks using 
three domestic stoves and three refriger¬ 
ators. Food was brought into camp to be 
cooked and served immediately as there 
was little storage space. Water was con¬ 
nected from a nearby shower house. 
Serving was completely paper, foam or 
plastic all summer — WOW — did we 
have a lot of garbage but unfortunately, 
we had no choice. We found it important 
to keep your staff posted on what is going 
on, they want and need to know. They 
also want to help out. We are grateful that 
all aspects of our insurance policy are up 
to date, this includes the “extra expense” 
clause. This is for such un-forseen 
expenses like paper and plastic service for 
the Summer, refrigerators and other 
equipment that must be bought for short 
term use that will never be used again, and 
other expenses too countless to mention. 


The Health Inspector was in frequently. 
They must ensure that everything is 
sanitary and that the food is good. Most 
of their policies we found normal and 
reasonable. Some days we were sure that 
our Inspectors’ superior had just said 
“this camp has just had a major tragedy, 
no one was hurt, but you make sure that 
nothing else happens!” and consequently, 
he seemed to be monitoring every detail 
under the sun! 

We were very fortunate to have lots of 
support from family and friends. Lisa’s 
parents, June and Cliff Labbett were 
sleeping soundly in Toronto that Tuesday 
morning at 6:30 a.m., needless-to-say 
their feet didn’t touch the ground for 
weeks after the fire. They were busy 
running here and there, buying pots, 
pans, cutlery, and dishes. They also made 
hundreds of phone calls to make the 
necessary emergency arrangements. Add 
to that the T-shirts they bought for all of 
the staff members. The shirts carried the 
slogan, “Together We’re Hot”. What a 
morale booster! We had support and 
practical help from many friends and 
family members to whom we will always 
be grateful. 

Hopefully, this information can prove 
helpful to someone one day. Although we 
wouldn’t wish a fire on anyone, if you 
ever do face the tragedy of a camp fire, 
then please contact us, we will do 
anything possible to help. 

Bruce and Lisa Wilson 

Summer (613) 375-6678 

Winter (416) 425-9796 

Quand un cas urgent frappe, c’est

des pensees et des emotions 
provoquees par un feu & Camp

GOING UP THE WALL 

En montant la mur 


L’usage d’une mur pour la montee comme activite 
challengeant et pour la pratique des d’exterites a profite au 
programme de Pioneer Ranch en Alberte. Bernie Woods, 
directeur des Camps Pioneer Ranch decrit le programme. 

For many years our camp had offered climbing trips to our 
more senior campers. These four to seven day trips were popular 
and offered the challenge and adventure of an alpine ascent in the 
Canadian Rockies. These programs were limited however by the 
distances involved, the training needed for campers, and the 
strength factor needed to participate in an alpine ascent. 
“Wouldn’t it be great” we thought, “if there was some way to 
involve more campers in the challenge of climbing?” 

All we needed was a site close to camp where it would be 
possible to satisfy a few conditions: 

1. Stable rock, with good access for campers to move from the 
top of the pitch to the bottom safely without being roped up. 

2. A pitch with routes for several ability levels and short 
enough to top rope all routes. 

3. A lower angle face on which to teach rappelling and an 
overhang on which to practise free rappells and prussicking. 

The problem was, the closest site was an hour away and only 
satisfied half the conditions. What we needed was a mountain 
right at camp if we were going to make this program option work. 
The solution had just become obvious. Some of us had worked 
with ways of creating simulated rock faces by bolting pieces of 
wood to an existing wall, (or chiseling holds in the natural rock 
facing on some buildings — a process not popular with the 
owners), or prefabricating laminated plywood panels and cutting 
holds into them, then fastening these to a wall. We had no such 
buildings at camp, but what if we built a freestanding 
structure...? 

The result was a three-sided tower, 35’ in height. Each face is 
16’ wide, enough room for two campers to be on the face at the 
same time. One face is vertical, and composed of 16 laminated 
plywood panels, which provide for a huge variety of routes for all 
skill levels. The second face is composed of rough sawn 3” x 10” 
boards and sits at a 75 degree angle so that it is easier to teach 
rappelling and mountain rescue techniques to campers. The third 
face is vertical and incorporates a 3’ overhang so that campers can 
gain experience in moving up and down over this type of obstacle 
and also practise prussicking. The foundation of the tower is 
several surplus telephone poles tied together with large timbers 
and then the whole structure stabilized with guy wires. Access to 
the top of the tower is provided by a ladder and platform system. 
At the top there are anchors for six ropes, two for each face. An 
added bonus is that an instructor on the top can quickly see what 
is happening on each face and offer assistance when necessary. 

We found that a coat of porch enamel with some sand mixed in 
provided for lots of protection and grip on the climbing faces, 

is* 


and that safety tread glued to the holds with contact cement was 
quite durable. The rough-sawn boards did not require any 
coating. 

The tower has proved to be a great asset and is very popular 
with all age groups. Best of all it has allowed us to offer the 
challenge of climbing to a wide variety of campers. Those 
campers going on a climbing trip are much better prepared for the 
adventure ahead. Trip leaders like the wall because it allows them 
to evaluate skill levels before the trip actually begins. Each year 
we discover new ways to use the wall to enhance the programs we 
offer at camp. 

You’ll have to excuse me now — it’s my turn to “go up the 
wall”! 

by Bernie Woods, 

Director of Pioneer Ranch Camps in Alberta. 

There is a network of ten Pioneer Camps across Canada, 
owned and operated by Inter-Varsity Christian Fellowship, a 
non-profit, interdenominational organization. Pioneer features 
both summer and winter programs designed to challenge and 
develop the whole person. 

Pioneer Ranch Camps were established in Alberta in 1951. The 
three Alberta Camps include: Pioneer Lodge, near Sundre, on the 
Red Deer River; Pioneer Ranch, near Rocky Mountain House, in 
Crimson Lake Provincial Park; and Peace Country Pioneer 
operating from Grande Prairie. 

The history and major program emphasis is instruction in western 
equitation. They also have programs in lake and whitewater 
canoeing, climbing, windsurfing, and an extensive tripping 
program on the eastern slopes of the Canadian Rockies.

Un etalage de programmes cabin afternoon program 


Si vous £tes employe & un camp ou si vous 6tes engage 
dans Timporte quelle manidre dans la jeunesse, vous 
reconnaissez le besoin d’une reserve presque in&puisable 
d’idees de programmation. On a le probl&me que comme le 
grandeur, l’£ge, le sexe, le temps permis, la situation et 
TSquipement changent, il y a aussi un changement d’id§e 
opportune. En-dessous, il y a de differentes situations ou 
de groupes avec un exemple de chacun. Faites une contre- 
fepreuve avec votre catalogue de ressources et utilisez-les 
quand vous avez I’opportunite. 

If you are on staff at a camp or involved in any way with youth 
then you recognize the need for a virtually endless supply of 
program ideas. The problem is that as size, age, sex, time frame, 
physical set up and equipment change then so, too, changes the 
particular program idea which is appropriate. Below are listed a 
number of different types of situations or groups along with an 
example of each. Cross check them against your personal 
catalogue of resources and use them when you can*. 

ENROUTE AND ARRIVAL ACTIVITY 

FAMOUS BUNKS 

Group: A cabin unit 

Equipment: Name Tags in Pairs (see below) 

As each person enters the room, he has a name tag pinned to his 
back. 

The object of the game is for each person to learn his identity 
and find his bunk. Each player is allowed to ask one “yes” or 
“no” question of any other player. At the same time, the two 
people introduce themselves (their real names!) and shake hands. 

Once a person has learned his identity, he tries to find his 
partner e.g. if he is Romeo, he looks for Juliet, which is pinned to 
a bunk in the cabin. 

The name on the name tag will be one half of a famous pair: 
eg. Antony and Cleopatra 
Abbott and Costello 
Bonnie and Clyde 


CABIN GAME 


STOMP 


This active game is not as brutal as its name suggests pro¬ 
vided it is played in stocking feet. 

The starting formation is a circle with all participants facing 
one another. The object is to eliminate other participants by 
landing on a portion of their foot with a portion of your own 
(not the heel). 

Participants are numbered. Number one has the first chance to 
take a stomp. He may jump and try to land on the foot of any 
neighbour. If he is successful then the stompee is out of that 
round. If he is unsuccessful then it is the turn of number two. 
Number one remains in the game. 

Other people may not jump out of the way until the stomper 
has jumped but must jump at the same time. This may be used to 
advantage. If the stomper pretends to jump but does not in fact 
leave the ground, then all those who actually jump are eliminated. 
A stomper’s turn is not over until he has made an actual jump. 

It will end with a head to head (or foot to foot) competition 
amidst much cheering and the winner’s only prize is safe feet and 
the opportunity to begin the next round. 


DROP ME A LINE 

This game can be a semi-active exploration hike in the woods 
or an exciting chase. One team has a head start and carries with it 
a handfull of 3 inch strings or brightly coloured yam. As they 
head off on their cross-country run they leave a trail of strings; 
each piece within view of the last. 

The second team enters the chase shortly after, collecting the 
strings as they go and announcing their position with loud calls. 

The first team continues until they run out of strings, return to 
the start, or are caught. 

OUTTRIP & OUTDOOR FUN 

TRICKY TREE TRAIL 

The counsellor needs some black thread for this game. He must 
go out beforehand and prepare some Tricky Trees. He might tie a 
maple leaf to the branch of a birch, a white pine sprig to a cedar, a 
balsam shoot to a hemlock. 

The campers hiking the trail should spot and remember the 
location of all the tricky trees. When they are finished the trail, 
they can announce how many ‘tricks’ they saw. 

Respotting the tricks and identifying the two types of trees will 
help with nature skills as well as providing lots of fun. 

BRAIN TEASER 

PEACHES, PEACHES 

“Peaches, peaches, very fine peaches, 

Very best peaches in town” 

This simple poem has confounded more people than any other 
we know. It is a must every time peaches are served at a mealtime 
and a common one many times when they’re not. 

Listeners are encouraged to “Repeat after me” and, clearing 
your throat, you recite the poem. 

At first, the audience will struggle with the structure of the lines 
or the position of your body, but as they master these they will 
still face the frustration of hearing from the leader, when they 
finish, “That was very close, but it wasn’t quite right”. 

The counsellor repeats it once more and clearing his throat he 
recites the poem. 

As a few listeners catch on, the fun and real confusion for 
others begins. A great way to end this stunt is to have all those 
who have learned the trick to come forward and recite the poem. 
They all clear their throats together (quite noticeably) and 
repeat: 

“Peaches, peaches, very fine peaches, 

Very best peaches in town” 

TABLE OR CIRCLE ACTIVITY 

WINK 

Another detective game for the amateur sleuth at the table, in a 
circle or in all-camp. 

One person is selected by some secret method to be a murderer. 
The counsellor may pick him, or he may draw a card, select a 
short stick, or pick the black marble from a bag. 

Now the fun begins. The murderer’s lethal weapon is his wink. 
The victim dies (dramatically please) five seconds after seeing the 
wink. 

Anyone spotting the crime may point the finger of accusation. 
If incorrect, they too, die but if they are correct another round 
begins.

CANADA CELEBRATES 
100 YEARS OF WILDLIFE 
CONSERVATION IN 1987 


SOME THOUGHTS FOR THE DAY 


RAINY DAY OR QUIET TIME ACTIVITY 


BIG BALL OF STRING 


If you scavenge and save every bit of string that comes along, 
you can accumulate a big ball, then pull it out at special times — 
rainy days, quiet times, etc. 

With some imagination, you can completely automate your 
cabin or tent. Set the amateur engineers to work to see if they can 
turn on the light or the tap, fetch a book, open and close 
windows, swat flies and send messages all from the comfort of 
their own bunks. 

Is it possible to use string to rig up an alarm clock for the 
morning or a booby trap to warn of prowlers? — Of course it is 
possible! Would we hand you a line? 


LARGE GROUP ACTIVITY 


MYSTERY TRAILS AND HUNTS 


“A journey of 1,000 (nautical) miles begins with the first step!” 
Get away ... to sea!” 


We owe this centennary to Sir John A. MacDonald who, on 
June 8, 1887, established the first Migratory Bird Sanctuary in the 
Western Hemisphere at Last Mountain Lake, south of 
Saskatoon. Twenty-four years later, on February 13, 1911, the 
first bird reserve in Alberta was set aside at Ministik Lake (south 
east of Edmonton). 

The Hon. Don Sparrow, Minister of Forestry, Lands, and 
Wildlife, has recognized the importance of these events and has 
endorsed the designation of 1987 as a special year for Wildlife 
Conservation for Alberta. 

We earnestly hope that your organization will become involved 
by helping us celebrate Wildlife ‘87. You may consider awarding 
recognition to members in your group who have made or are 
making a contribution to wildlife conservation. Or you may want 
to undertake a project to display to the public your involvement 
with wildlife. We have, for your perusal, enclosed a list of other 
possible activities. These and those suggested by your executive 
may stimulate someone in your group to implement one or more 
of these ideas. It is the spirit of cooperation that will ensure 
Wildlife ‘87 is a success. 


WHEN A CHILD ASKS DIFFICULT QUESTIONS, IN¬ 
VENTION IS THE NECESSITY OF MOTHER. 

Maugham S. Wright 


THE ROAD TO SUCCESS IS ALWAYS UNDER CON¬ 
STRUCTION. 

Hubert Dorfensplat 


TO TRAVEL HOPEFULLY IS A BETTER THING THAN 
TO ARRIVE. 

Robert Louis Stevenson 


THE FAULTS OF OTHERS ARE LIKE HEADLIGHTS OF 
AN AUTOMOBILE. THEY ONLY SEEM MORE GLARING 
THAN OUR OWN. 

Carson Highbeam 


WX CAN MAKX A DIFFXRXNCX! XVXR FXXL WX ARX 
NOT IMPORTANT? THAT WX’RX JUST ANOTHXR KXY 
ON LIFX’S TYPXWRITXR? WXLL, JUST SXX WHAT 
HAPPXNS WHXN ONX KXY IS MISSING. SUBSTITUTXS

X Mark Suspott 


HE WHO CUTS HIS OWN WOOD IS WARMED TWICE. 

Perce Pyre 


WHEN WE PUT OURSELVES IN THE OTHER PERSON’S 
PLACE, WE’RE LESS LIKELY TO WANT TO PUT HIM IN 
HIS PLACE. 

U. Ken Countonit 


Each camper unit seeks information at predetermined locations 
to solve a mystery, gain points, or acquire rewards. 

The advantage of this type of event is that counsellors and their 
cabins can stay together and participate as a group at their own 
pace. 


e.g. 

Detective — Each station is staffed by a mysterious character 
who can reveal a clue to the mystery at hand. Clues are 
assembled and finally detectives file a warrant. 

Comic Book Hunt — Staff at stations show a single clue to 
their comic book identity, (eg. freckles — Archie, rifle — 
Elmer Fudd). They can answer three questions with either Yes 
or No. Camper unit must then guess their identity. How many 
characters can you identify? 

Where’s Our Snack — Treasure hunts following rhyming 
clues to the next station and the next station and finally to 
snack! 


Stalk The Animals — This is one of many ideas that could be 
used to “Hunt the Staff*’. Staff members, in costumes de¬ 
signed to make them look like animals (e.g. lion, monkey, 
chipmunk, bear, tortoise, rabbit), find hiding places in a 
habitat suitable for their species of animal. Campers find the 
staff and bring them back to an enclosed pen where they 
might perform some animal trick or feat. 

These program descriptions are taken from Lead On . . . 

Counsellor, a Camp Tawingo Publication by Jack Pearse, John 

Jorgenson, Jane McCutcheon and Pat Pearse.

NORTHERN ILLINOIS 
UNIVERSITY 

Department of Curriculum and Instruction 


ASSISTANTSHIPS IN OUTDOOR 
TEACHER EDUCATION 


Northern Illinois University 


More than a dozen graduate teaching assistantships are 
available at the Field Campus in Outdoor Teacher Education at 
Northern Illinois University for the 1987 - 88 school year. 

These assistantships involve outdoor teaching at the Lorado 
Taft Field Campus, Oregon, Illinois. Because the teaching is 
primarily with public school students and university juniors and 
seniors, priority is given to those applicants who have had several 
years of experience in the elementary or secondary public schools 
or outdoor schools. Applicants who have nature centre and/or 
camping experience will also be considered. 

The assistantships pay a stipend of S320 per month for nine 
months and include a waiver of tuition for three semesters. Room 
and board is included for the fall and spring semesters when 
groups are in residence. 

Applications and further information may be received by 
writing to Dr. Clifford E. Knapp, P.O. Box 299, Lorado Taft 
Field Campus, Oregon, IL 61061. (815) 732-2111. 

For a complete listing of twenty-four courses and degree 
opportunities offered in Outdoor Teacher Education, write to 
Dr. Knapp at the address above.

SUBSCRIPTION INFORMATION 

Canadian Camping Magazine is the official publication of the Canadian Camping Association. 
Editorial offices of the Magazine are located at R.R. # 1, Huntsville, Ontario, P0A 1K0. 

Membership in the C.C.A., as a result of membership in a provincial camping association, 
includes a subscription to the Magazine. Non member subscription is $8.00/year. Single issue price 
is $2.00. Make cheques payable to the Canadian Camping Association. Send subscriptions, sub¬ 
missions, or address changes to the editorial offices. 

Canadian Camping Magazine is published four times yearly. Deadlines for submissions arc 
October 1, December 1, February 15 and May 1. Material in Canadian Camping Magazine may 
not be reproduced in any form without the expressed written permission of the editor. Copyright 
1986 Canadian Camping Association.
